name: AI in Health Care Delivery
blurb: How hospitals, practices and payers use AI in patient care and its administration.
title: AI in Health Care Delivery
answer: AI in care delivery is spreading but unevenly. About a third of US hospitals reported using AI in a 2025 national study, ambient AI scribes are the fastest growing tool, and the main constraints are privacy rules, evidence that tools help patients, and the work of fitting them into clinical routines.

reading.body:
About a third of US hospitals were using AI in 2025, and another quarter planned to start within a year. That is real adoption, but it leaves most hospitals on the outside, and it says nothing about how deeply the tools are used where they exist.

The pattern is that AI enters care delivery through administration and documentation before clinical judgment. Ambient scribes are the fastest growing tool because they sit beside the visit rather than inside the decision, and the constraints named are privacy rules, evidence of patient benefit, and the work of fitting tools into clinical routines. Those are not compute constraints. They are legal, evidentiary, and organisational ones, which is why adoption is uneven across institutions rather than uniform across the country.

The regulatory line matters for what comes next. The FDA's 2022 guidance on clinical decision support software sets which tools are regulated as devices, so the same capability can be a documentation aid or a regulated product depending on how it is framed. The cited literature runs from 2009 to 2023, and the most cited paper is from 2019, so the research base predates the current generation of language models.

What the data does not cover is cost, staffing, or outcomes. It names one vendor, OpenAI, and one deployment list, and it does not say whether any of these tools improved patient care.

sections.body: Start with tools that remove administrative work, documentation and authorisation, where the evidence of benefit is clearest and the clinical risk lowest, and require a business associate agreement before any tool touches patient data.

developments.text: A national study in JAMA Network Open found 31.5 percent of US hospitals were current AI users and 24.7 percent planned adoption within a year.
OpenAI launched OpenAI for Healthcare with deployments at institutions including Boston Children's Hospital, Cedars-Sinai, HCA Healthcare and UCSF.
The FDA issued final guidance on clinical decision support software, setting which tools are regulated as devices.
